Neonates of the Eastern fiddler ray emerge from their egg cases at a total length of 27 centimeters [Lb = 27 centimeters], a modest size that reflects the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent development within a protected capsule. Upon hatching, these young individuals are immediately capable of independent foraging on small benthic invertebrates, a critical transition to the exotrophic phase of life. Field surveys conducted in temperate Australian estuaries indicate that the gestation period, during which embryos develop within the female through a process of yolk-sac absorption, spans approximately 380 days [ab = approximately 380 days] when ambient water temperatures average 20.7 °C [T = 20.7 °C]. This protracted developmental interval is characteristic of many batoid elasmobranchs and is believed to contribute to the relatively large size of the pups at parturition, which enhances their survival prospects against predation in shallow nursery habitats. The emergence at such an advanced stage of development allows the pups to avoid the most vulnerable early life stages that plague smaller, less developed offspring in other chondrichthyan lineages.

As the Eastern fiddler ray progresses through its juvenile phase, it undergoes a sustained period of somatic growth that culminates in the attainment of its ultimate total length. The maximum recorded total length for this species is 120 centimeters [Li = 120 centimeters], a value derived from large, presumably aged adults captured during long-term monitoring programs off the coast of New South Wales. This asymptotic dimension, substantially larger than that observed in many congeners, corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 10,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 10,000 grams], a relationship that aligns closely with the species' robust, dorso-ventrally flattened body plan. The energetic demands of achieving such dimensions require consistent feeding on a diet rich in crustaceans and molluscs, and the species appears to channel the majority of its ingested energy into structural growth during the early juvenile years. Field observations suggest that growth rates decelerate markedly once individuals approach this maximal size threshold.

Sexual maturation in the Eastern fiddler ray is a gradual process that proceeds differently between the sexes, with males typically attaining reproductive competency at a smaller overall dimension. Detailed examination of gonad development and clasper calcification in preserved specimens has established that females reach puberty at a total length of 76.4 centimeters [Lp = 76.4 centimeters], a size at which ovarian follicles begin to mature and vitellogenesis is initiated. Males, in contrast, achieve puberty at a total length of 67.5 centimeters [Lp = 67.5 centimeters], a difference that likely reflects the earlier energetic investment required for the development of claspers and sperm production. These lengths fall within the range of 65 to 70 centimeters (65-70 centimeters) [Lp = 65-70 centimeters] reported in earlier studies of male maturity for this species, confirming the robustness of this estimate. The onset of gonad maturation marks a pivotal shift in energy allocation, as resources previously dedicated primarily to somatic expansion are increasingly diverted toward the production of gametes and reproductive behaviors.

Reproductive output in the Eastern fiddler ray is relatively modest when compared to many teleost fishes, yet it is characteristic of a K-selected life-history strategy typical of elasmobranchs. Gravid females produce litters that range from 4 to 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4 to 7 pups per litter], with the frequency of pupping events estimated at approximately one litter per year [F_R_i = approximately one litter per year] under the prevailing thermal conditions of their subtropical habitat. This reproductive rate has been documented in captive populations maintained at a stable water temperature of 20.7 °C [T = 20.7 °C], where females exhibit consistent annual breeding cycles. The maximum daily reproduction rate of this species, calculated as approximately 5.3 pups per 365-day period [Ri = approximately 5.3 pups per 365-day period], reflects the slow pace of reproduction typical of elasmobranchs. The combination of moderate litter sizes and an extended gestation period constrains the species' maximum annual reproductive output, but the resulting pups are large and well-provisioned, enhancing their immediate survival. This slow pace of reproduction makes the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as population recovery from depletion can take many years.

Longevity data for the Eastern fiddler ray, derived from tag-recapture studies and vertebral band counts, indicate a maximum lifespan spanning 26 years [am = 26 years] when individuals experience the thermal regime of their natural environment at 20.7 °C [T = 20.7 °C]. This exceptional lifespan, which is among the highest recorded for Australian rhinobatids, allows for multiple reproductive events over an adult's lifetime, partially compensating for the low annual fecundity. The species' slow pace of life is further underscored by the protracted developmental timeline from birth to reproductive maturity. At the end of life, senescence in this species manifests as a gradual decline in reproductive condition and an increased susceptibility to parasitic infections, rather than a sudden physiological collapse, marking a prolonged post-reproductive period in some of the oldest documented individuals. The combination of a long pre-reproductive phase, modest litter sizes, and an extended adult life reinforces the profile of the Eastern fiddler ray as a species with a bet-hedging strategy adapted to stable, resource-predictable environments.
